title: Microdecode path sampling chronicle
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an exploratory set of CPU-side samples and microbench experiments focused on the smallest, high-volume request path we call the 'microdecode' flow. The goal is to pin down dominant CPU contributors (token/lexical scanning, header/body parse, scheduler wakeups, Python interpreter overhead) for ~50–200B token short requests (typical tiny-chat and single-prompt completion workloads). We want actionable mitigations (fastpath C surface, lighter parse, threadpool tuning, reduced GIL influence).

Background and why this matters:
- Microdecode flow dominates tail-latency for many production customers: median is low, but p95/p99 spikes partially attributable to CPU-side preproc.
- We've seen intermittent spikes when concurrent small requests increase. Existing sampling traces hint at a mix of: repeated UTF-8 scanning, JSON header parsing, Python bytecode dispatch, and some costly syscalls during allocator contention and thread wake.

High-level hypothesis (prioritized):
1) Repeated UTF-8/lex scanning in the fast path (lexer-style scanning for input booleans, numbers, short strings) is a measurable contributor — we can gain by merging a tiny C scanner and short-circuiting full JSON parse.
2) Python threadpool handoffs + GIL acquisition cost for the preproc chain creates jitter under bursty arrival patterns.
3) Small allocations (temporary buffers) and jemalloc arena contention cause unpredictability; reducing alloc churn should reduce p99.
4) Syscall noise (clock_gettime, futex, epoll_wait/ctl) from scheduling and polling amplifies tail events.

Experiment matrix executed (notes):
- Workloads: synthetic tiny-completions using benchmark-client v0.21 hitting local dev instance with --qps 800/1600/3200, concurrency 64/128. Payloads: 60–200 bytes prompt, headers include metadata (x-customer-id, x-route-hash).
- Builds: baseline runtime@main + branch microdecode-fastpath (C lexer extension + short-json-parser) + pyshim-coop-yield (cooperative yield points around blocking IO) + allocator-config (jemalloc tunings).
- Collection tools: perf (200Hz sample), eBPF offcpu, python sampling profiler (Yappi, wall-time), and a lightweight event sampling harness (userland stack-sampling every 1ms for p99 window).

Representative commands used:
- perf: perf record -F 200 -a -g -- sleep 120; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > perf.folded; flamegraph.pl perf.folded > perf.svg
- offcpu: bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { @[comm] = count(); }' -c './bench-client --...'

Key observations (summary):
- Percent-of-samples: In baseline, ~32% of CPU samples during request handling map to Python interpreter frames (frame evaluation loop + call to _parse_headers), ~18% to our C JSON library (rapidly scanning header bytes), ~12% to UTF-8 validation/scanning routines, and ~10% to kernel syscalls (futex/epoll).
- Under the C-lexer fastpath branch, Python-frame samples drop to ~19% and UTF-8 scanning samples drop to ~4%. End-to-end median latency improved by ~8–12% at 1600 QPS; p99 improved by ~18%.
- Cooperative-yield pyshim reduced timer/scheduler syscall bursts: observed futex counts down 22% and small improvement of 6% at p95, but p99 unchanged unless combined with C-lexer.
- Jemalloc tuning (per-thread arenas and MADV behaviour) reduced short-lived allocation time for the preproc stack by ~15% in allocation hot loops; combined effect visible on p99 when concurrency >128.

Interesting flamegraph patterns: (text summary)
- Baseline: tall stack including PyEval_EvalFrameEx -> parse_headers -> PyBytes_FromStringAndSize -> cjson_scan -> utf8_scan. Many samples cluster at frame dispatch points and PyObject refcount ops.
- Fastpath: tall frame shifts into c_lexer_tokenize and very shallow Python wrappers; call overhead eliminated for many common tokens (strings, ints, simple punctuation).

Microbench numbers (representative):
- Baseline at 1600 QPS, concurrency 64: median 22ms, p95 58ms, p99 120ms. CPU utilization ~82% of a 16-vCPU worker.
- Fastpath+C-lexer: median 19.5ms, p95 48ms, p99 98ms. CPU util marginally lower but requests processed more smoothly.
- Pyshim-coop only: median 20.3ms, p95 55ms, p99 115ms.
- Combined (C-lexer + jemalloc + pyshim): median 18.9ms, p95 44ms, p99 81ms.

Qualitative notes from sampling traces:
- Short-circuiting the full JSON parse for small headers avoids both Python allocation churn and a large fraction of visitations into cjson.
- Many Python samples are actually waiting in interpreter for small C extension calls to return — reducing the transition frequency reduces overhead.
- There are cases where repeated small reads trigger syscalls repeatedly (epoll_ctl churn). Batching or coalescing socket operations in the accept/ingest path reduces syscall noise.

Risks and unknowns:
- C-lexer correctness surface: must preserve exact semantics for unicode escapes and surrogate pairs. Need fuzz tests and interop tests with real customer traffic.
- Long-term maintainability: adding another specialized C path increases test surface and porting effort across platforms (macOS vs Linux vs musl).
- Interactions with fallback models/routes: fastpath must gracefully drop to existing JSON parser for rare cases; ensure perf overhead of detection is minimal.

Actionable proposals (short-term to medium-term):
1) Landing a guarded C-lexer for header + small-body fast path: feature flag disabled by default, enabled on a subset of hosts. Add fidelity tests to ensure parity. (Owner: Asha)
2) Add sampling-based flamegraphs to nightly perf CI for microdecode workload (generate p95/p99 regression alerts). (Owner: Miguel)
3) Apply jemalloc per-thread arena tweak to dedicated worker image and run soak at 2000+ QPS for 72h. (Owner: Priya)
4) Prototype socket operation coalescing in request acceptor (mini-batch accept and deferral logic) to reduce epoll_ctl churn. (Owner: Ethan)
5) Add stress fuzzing for unicode escape corner cases to prevent regression in C-lexer. (Owner: Asha + Research)

Short checklist for PR and rollout:
- [ ] Unit + fuzz tests green
- [ ] Canary on dedicated infra (10% of tiny-request fleet)
- [ ] Telemetry: add metric for "fastpath-hit-rate", fastpath-fallthrough-count, and transition cost histogram
- [ ] Post-canary perf A/B after 24h and 72h (collect p50/p95/p99, CPU cycles, syscall rates)

Open questions for discussion in next sync:
- How do we attribute Python-sample time precisely to GIL vs waiting on C extension? Need a combined offcpu + interpreter tracing approach.
- Should we invest in a small vectorized UTF-8/SIMD scanner in Rust instead of C for memory-safety and easier cross-platform builds? Tradeoffs?
- Is there an upper QPS point where batching (coalescing) harms latency for single-request SLAs? Need microbench for tail vs throughput tradeoff.

Appendix: quick repro steps for engineers
1) Checkout branch microdecode-fastpath.
2) Build with: make -C runtime CFLAGS="-O3 -march=native"
3) Start local worker: ./runtime/bin/worker --config=dev-fastpath.toml &
4) Run bench-client: ./bench-client --target localhost:8080 --qps 1600 --concurrency 64 --payload ./test-payloads/micro.json
5) Collect perf: perf record -F 200 -p $(pgrep -f worker) -g -- sleep 60; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded

Notes-to-self: keep iteration lightweight, focus on observable wins in p99 for real traffic. Prioritize correctness and safety over an aggressive fastpath if either causes inconsistent outputs.

End of note.
